audio3/energy-hero.mp3: Height becomes speed. Roll a ball down from a height and clock it at the bottom. The speed follows the height by a square-root rule.
audio3/energy-try.mp3: Try this. Choose a start height and tap Release. The speed gate records a dot. Measure at three or more heights. Fit the number. The line curves over: four times the height only doubles the speed. Predict the speed from a 4 metre ramp, then test it.
audio3/energy-rule.mp3: The rule in words. A higher start gives more speed, but not in a straight line. Four times the height only doubles the speed. That pattern is a square root. So the speed is a number, times the square root of the height. As a formula: speed equals a number times the square root of the height.
audio3/energy-saw.mp3: What you saw. Height stored becomes speed paid out. The number you fitted is the square root of two times g, about 4.4 on Earth, so the 9.8 from the falling lessons is hiding inside it. Square both sides and the rule reads speed squared equals 2 times g times height. That is the energy idea from Level 1, now with a number on it. If nothing rubs, it tells you how fast a skier is going at the bottom of a hill, whatever the skier weighs.
audio3/wave-hero.mp3: Ripples and rules. Dip faster and the ripples bunch together. The gap between them follows a rule you can fit.
audio3/wave-try.mp3: Try this. Pick shallow or deep water, set the dipper frequency, and tap Measure. The ruler shows the gap between ripples. Measure at three or more frequencies. Fit the number. The line is a curve that dives and then flattens. Predict the gap at 10 ripples a second and test it. Then switch the water and try again.
audio3/wave-rule.mp3: The rule in words. Faster dipping packs the ripples closer together. Twice the dips each second, half the gap. So the gap is one fixed number, divided by the frequency. As a formula: gap equals a number divided by the frequency.
audio3/wave-saw.mp3: What you saw. The number you fitted is how fast the ripples travel. It belongs to the water, not the dipper: deeper water carries ripples faster. Dip faster and the ripples are made faster than they can spread out, so they bunch up. The same rule governs sound and light. A note of 440 hertz travels at 343 metres per second, so its wavelength is 343 divided by 440, a bit under 0.8 metres.
